utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to greet the accused. I'd like to greet their counsels, the representatives of the Office of the Prosecution, as well as all those assisting us in the courtroom. I'd like to give the floor to the Registrar for an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution has submitted its objections to documents tendered by 2D via Witness Davor Korac. This list shall be given Exhibit IC988. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Witness, I'd like to welcome you as well, and I'm going to give the floor to Ms. Nozica without further adieu, who will finish her in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I am now going to ask you -- I have about 50 minutes left, which is not good either for you or for me. However, I'm going to ask you to provide as short answers as possible with regard to the documents and the questions that I'm going to ask you, because we will be talking about the things which the Trial Chamber is familiar with. Could you look at 2D324 in your second binder, this is where we left it off yesterday. 324. Just for the transcript, 2D324 is the number, 2D324. Did you find it? Mr. Bagaric, this is a report by Dr. Ljubic about the evacuation of BiH members. This took place in Medjugorje on the 12th of June, 1993, and they were evacuated for further treatment. Were you made aware of that, and were such evacuations frequent?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is one of them. I can't tell you how many there were, but it was a common occurrence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I would now kindly ask you to look at the following document, which is P2703, which should be the following document in your binder. At least that's what I think. This is another report by the European Monitors, dated 11 June 1993. Under item 5 of this report, you can see that the team visited the west bank and they conveyed a letter of the Corps Command about the request for medicines that we discussed yesterday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now can you please look at the following document, again issued by the European Monitors. P2731 is the document number.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a report dated 12 June in which it says that the medicines under item 5, and it is on page 1 in both English and Croatian, that the drugs and medicines from the HVO hospital have been dispatched to the hospital on the east bank?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, a UN member got killed while transporting the medicines over there, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you now look at 2D276.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, this is a letter dated 14 July. This is your letter in which you say that on the 13th of July in Domanovic, en route to Capljina, while transporting the wounded, the driver of the ambulance was killed from an ambush at close range, and Nurse Vesna Mijatovic was seriously wounded. You are the one who signed this, together with Dr. Sarac. What is this, Dr. Bagaric? Is this a protest letter? There's no addressee. Who was it sent to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a case which unfortunately happened, and there were several such cases. My colleague, Nurse Lilija Zerno [phoen], was also killed from an ambush while she was assisting the wounded. She was also killed from an ambush set up by the Bosniak Muslim Army, and she was a nurse. We had a total of 37 killed medical personnel of the HVO, and this is actually an address to the general public, as the first figure in the healthcare, together with my colleague, Ivan Sarac, who was in charge of the civilian healthcare that I mentioned yesterday. We're both appealing to everybody to prevent such things from happening. This is an appeal to the general public. We are appealing to everybody in Herceg-Bosna to abide by the Geneva Conventions on behalf of the HVO Medical Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, in Domanovic, on the 13th of July, 1993 -- maybe we have to clarify this. Who could it have been who could have opened fire, which army?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I already said that it was the Muslims, the BiH Army. They set up an ambush and they opened fire and, unfortunately, killed the person in question, the person referred to herein.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please look at 2D4255 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a request which has already been admitted into evidence. Again, we are following a temporal sequence. This is a request in which you requested from UNPROFOR, from the Spanish Battalion, that is, to mediate with the Muslim side regarding the accommodation of civilians and women in the war hospital in Mostar and in other hospitals, and you say at the end that you are doing this for humanitarian reasons and that you are asking for this not to be given any political background. Is this one of your requests, and did you receive any reply to this request of yours?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is one of my requests. This is a very serious -- a very important request, and in a certain way I already spoke about this yesterday. I sent it to the international community, to the representatives thereof, in agreement with Commander Petkovic and Defence Minister Mr. Stojic. Why did I do this, why was it me who did it? Because I was the first person in the healthcare of the HVO, and I believe that if a doctor appealed to everybody to treat people in town together, if I was the one who wanted to make the hospital an executorial [as interpreted] building, as it were, and that the representatives of the International Red Cross should enter it and control its work, then I believe that nobody would ever be able to refuse such a request, especially if we were talking about the east side of Mostar, which was in a more difficult situation than us when it came to the healthcare of the wounded. However, unfortunately again we did not receive a reply to this letter, again.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I would now kindly ask to be able to correct the number before Judge Trechsel's intervention. This was document number 2D455. The number is reflected erroneously in the transcript. Very well, then. And now I would kindly ask you to look at 2D328.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a confirmation or a receipt for a certain quantity of blood that was provided to the UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned that yesterday. This is one of our -- how shall I put it -- one of our very important attempts to open the lines of communications in order to help the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just been warned that P2703 is under seal. We just saw it on the screen, P2703, and I believe that it is of some importance for this to be stressed out that this is a document under seal and it was published a minute ago. And also 2731, the same thing applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed. The Registrar told me that the document had not been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you to look at 2D333. Mr. Bagaric, in this courtroom we have already heard Ms. Sally Backer. Could you please confirm whether you handed over to Ms. Sally Backer, as it says in this document, a vehicle for the transport of the wounded from the left bank of the Neretva to the war hospital, Mostar? Was that one of your missions or activities aimed at helping the wounded in the hospital on the left bank?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Sally Backer requested our support to go to the other side, and there was a possibility for her to be killed. She wanted to take some of our patients, a woman and some children. She wanted to go through the front-lines, and she wanted us to provide her with a vehicle. We did so, we gave her a vehicle, and I'm convinced that on one occasion she did not succeed. She actually made two or three attempts. On one occasion, she failed because they wouldn't allow her on the east side to implement her attempt. They even seized the vehicle. However, I know for a fact that she made two successful journeys and that she took the children and their mothers and she brought them over to our side, as it were, and then we allowed her to contact the Split Hospital. The Split Hospital took the children and continued their treatment, and then from there they went into a third country somewhere in Europe. I don't know where.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, skip the following document. I have to reduce the number of documents that I want to show you. The next one is an exhibit. Can you now please look at 2D23 [as interpreted], which is also under seal, I emphasise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, item 5 on page 2 in the English version, it is item --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, the interpreters have asked that the number please be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Thank you very much. P2923, P2923.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Have you found the document, Ms. Bagaric?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now we have the correct number in the transcript. Let's just confirm. We saw your letters, and here we see a report submitted by the European Monitors, and under item 5, in the second paragraph, you are sending a proposal to them about setting up a hospital on the west side which would function as a joint hospital for the treatment of both ones and the others. This is a confirmation that the international organisations did indeed receive your proposal?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a confirmation to that effect. And if I can just briefly comment, it says here -- or, rather, it is confirmed here that this is it. However, there is a claim here. It says that in the exchange of doctors with the hospital on the east side, I personally would not accept everything until we ensured the freedom of movement for the HVO doctors who had to work in the hospitals in Travnik, Konjic, in Zenica and so on and so forth. I don't know what kind of interpretation that was, how they interpreted our letters. However, I spoke about that yesterday and I said that they did not have any volunteers who would be willing to go to the east side, irrespective of their ethnic background, and that was the major problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The next and the last document in the series speaks about that. It is also under seal. It is P2929. Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: P2929. It should be the next document in the series.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Under item 1, you can see that this is referred to. This is an exhibit. I would like to draw your attention to the exchange of doctors and the reason for that. It says here Bruno Stojic, the chief of the HVO Medical Staff, agreed with "our proposal in principle." It seems that the International Monitors and the European community had a problem with positions and functions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they made a mistake, because at the time Mr. Stojic was the head of the department?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we go to the following page, item 3: "The reason that M2 Mostar is dealing with this problem, and not the UNHCR or the International Red Cross is dealing with that, is because of the fact that in Mostar only team M2 is visiting daily both sides and many times the hospitals. It seems to be for the last couple of weeks the aforementioned international organisations do not want to deal with this kind of problems." Mr. Bagaric, does this confirm exactly what you were talking about, and that is the position of the international organisations towards the medical problems that you had to deal with?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I allow for the fact that in a way this is somebody's subjective viewpoint. However, I was under the same impression very often, so what I can say is that I agree with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, we'll now move on to another area, and we're going to deal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a follow-up question. Clearly, the documents we have seen demonstrate the efforts you have made to establish a joint hospital between the two parties in order to treat all the wounded of the war. With several other witnesses and with the support of hundreds of documents, we've looked into the East and West Mostar hospital issue or hospitals issue, and we found out that there were several international organisations working even in the East Mostar Hospital, foreigners, physicians who were there to assist, and one of the organisations is Medecins Sans Frontieres. Now, you -- we know that there were all those people and the International Red Cross as well. Why, knowing this, have you not turned to them so that under the auspices of the Red Cross, this joint hospital would be established, treating everybody, rather than approaching the Spanish Battalion, so to say, requesting it to play a focal role? Because we know there were foreign physicians who were there with organisations, with the assistance of their countries, who could have set up that hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you for that question. When it comes to the International Red Cross, it is an institution without any force and no power in the area; no weapons, no equipment, and no -- no protection for itself, no security for itself. That's why we went to the Spanish Battalion first, because we had relatively good and I can even say excellent cooperation with them, because they enabled us to go up to Konjic on that occasion and all the places there and organise the meeting, and Mr. Morales, I remember him well as having been a very serious person and somebody who was in a position to help us. So I say with full responsibility that with this piece of paper of ours, our request, independently of what it says, that we contacted the UN, that we were known to the International Red Cross as well. However, quite simply, we did not receive a response, no answer, so they weren't able to do anything without UNPROFOR, and UNPROFOR most probably could not put this into practice because it did not receive an affirmative answer. I'm sure that they did try, but once they failed, they left it at that. So this is a rare example, perhaps even in the history of warfare in general, and it was published and this example put forward in a scholarly and journal as an example of how an international organisation, and the other side, too, did not respond to the first attempt made at establishing communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, and now finally I'm going to ask you a set of questions having to do with the detention centres and the role of the Health Sector in those centres. Mr. Bagaric, at the collegium of the Defence Department, did they discuss military prisons and detention centres at all?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember and when I was there, when I attended the senior staff meetings or collegiums, they discussed it on one occasion and I remember that occasion very well. I think it was at the beginning of September. However, up until then, our doctors, and when I say "our doctors," I mean the doctors in the brigades in the military districts and also our physicians in the Health Sector who were in charge of preventive medical care, led by Dr. Curic, they went to those centres. And I was one of them, although strictly speaking, that wasn't part of my job.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, why did the Health Sector, as you say, and Mr. Curic, which is the Infectology and Epidemiological Service, why did they visit the prisons and detention centres?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to under this fully, you have to know what the setup was, the system, the units on the ground, the overall situation on the ground, and so on and so forth. So Dr. Curic, who was at the head of this sector of ours, in a way provided professional support, because I think that he was the only infectious disease specialist there and in the territory where the HVO units were located, which means that he visited the units, toured the units, and the doctors in those units, but also he took care to see that they had clean water to drink, a good water supply, and everything else that the prevention of disease involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: To the best of your recollections, Mr. Curic and the service that he headed, did they visit the refugee centres at all?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And did they visit all the places where large numbers of people congregated?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've just confirmed that, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, did you consider that these centres, and you've already told us that Mr. Curic visited them, that you went to one of them, and we'll come to that later on, but did you consider that, organisationally speaking, these centres belonged to the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And you said that you visited one of the detention centres. Could you explain to the Court where you went and when you went?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went once to the Heliodrom, and I think it was -- well, I can't give you a precise date, but it might have been in mid-July 1993 or thereabouts. And a member of the Helsinki Board came to visit me, and a professor for public health, Slobodan Lang from Zagreb. When they came to visit me, then the two of us went there together, and I asked him to use his connections and also, based on his experience and knowledge, to help us so that we could help the doctors in turn who were already involved with the specific prison that you've just mentioned. So that was a time of open warfare. There was an open conflict and war going on, and we didn't know what the morrow would bring. So we weren't prepared properly, nor were we able to deal with the situation. And it was an outcome of the war that we did not wish to see, a detention centre or a camp, but had I been involved, I would of course have had more experience than I do now. However, with the help of Dr. Lang and all the people down there who were directly in charge of the centre, and for those of us who came from outside and supported those people there with our knowledge and generally our moral support, we and Mr. Curic, I think, succeeded in what we intended to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I think you've also already answered the question I want to ask you next, because we have seen reports to that effect, but let me ask you whether you were in the detention centres of Gabela and Dretelj ever.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As I was saying, we've already seen some reports here in court, and we see that certain measures were proposed, put forward in those reports and some of the orders that you signed, but tell us now: Whose job was it to put those measures into practice, Mr. Bagaric?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, in the reports that were clearly written, written in detail, setting out the system, and I'd like to thank Mr. Curic for that, first and foremost, it is clear that in the Healthcare Sector it was our health staff that were involved, those who were in the units themselves and who was -- who supervised those centres, and when it came to all other aspects, logistics, of course, for the units and the military districts to which these centres belonged.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We'll go through some of these reports in due course, although we've seen quite a lot of them in the courtroom, and we had quite a number of your own orders. Now, is it your impression that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Nozica. I would like to ask one or a few questions. Dr. Bagaric, who authorised you to enter Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, it was the time of open conflict and all-out war, and I was the head of the Medical Service of the Croatian Defence -- of the HVO, and I never actually heard of anybody in official terms establishing the centre. I saw this as part of the facts that I told you about, and I thought that as a doctor, I would go there with Mr. Lang, or Dr. Lang, and we simply got into a car. I know that you must find this a little unusual, but that's how things were. We just got into a car and drove off and went there, and at the entrance, I happened to meet a young man who was standing at the door and said we wouldn't be allowed to enter or I wouldn't be allowed to enter. And I said that I was a physician and that it was my intention to go inside. And then I assumed that somebody recognised me, and they said, Let the doctor go, let the doctor pass. So Lang and I went inside without any formal or official permission to do so. That was what the situation was like. It was a really chaotic time, a chaotic situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you wearing your uniform or were you in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the war, as I was the chief of the Medical Corps of the HVO, I think I was always in uniform, and I had the International Red Cross emblem on my uniform so that people could recognise me as being a doctor, and of course without any weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And the man standing at the entrance at Heliodrom was also wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. You have spoken of "our people" dealing with the situation there. I'm asking you these questions because you have said a short while ago that the detention centre was not within the province of the Defence Department, of the military, but what you are telling us now rather points to the contrary; namely, that the authority which was above Heliodrom at that time was the military branch of HVO, which would be the Department for Defence. What do you -- what is your reaction to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say or correct, in a way, what I said earlier on to make things quite clear. I often use the term "our patients," "we," "our doctors," and when I say this, these first-person plural, I am referring to my colleagues, regardless of where they live. But those doctors were not in my Health Sector, nor were they in the Defence Sector. They were out on the ground in units or the brigade or in the military district. So I think that's what I wanted to clear up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So you seem to stay with the view that the Heliodrom Centre at that moment was not under the authority of the Department of Defence. If that is so, under what authority was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did not say nor do I know at that time under whose authority it was, as such. What I, in fact, said was that as a physician myself, who was in charge of dealing with HVO healthcare at the top level, I felt a need to go there. I never saw an order to that effect or an order establishing the centre in the first place, nor did I ever attend any meetings discussing the formation of this prison or any other, or the Centre for Isolation as they were called, or whatever. I really didn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I leave it at that for the moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the issue of the Heliodrom Centre is a key issue to this case. Heliodrom is the very cornerstone of this case. You told us that you were in charge of the Health Sector in the Defence Department. As a doctor, therefore, with Slobodan Lang, your colleague, you went to the Heliodrom. And you told us - this is what you answered Judge Trechsel - that before you went there, you did not know how that centre was operating. This is something you discover when you go there, if I understood you correctly. I do not want to catch you by surprise. It may be the Prosecutor's role, but I won't do that. I'm neutral, and I'm trying to understand the gist of this case. We've already heard witnesses who described what happened in Heliodrom. This has been described for us. You went to the Heliodrom, and did you realise that it is a centre where there are people who are detained, and hence this raises the question of the responsibility of the Medical Service of the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're talking about July here, we're dealing with July. It's not September, October, November, it's July. And in July, in July, well, Heliodrom couldn't be hidden. You couldn't hide Heliodrom. I knew about Heliodrom, and I knew that it was a military base or barracks and allegedly a prison, a central prison, as such. But after the conflict between the BH Army and the HVO in Mostar, that is to say, when the Muslim Bosniaks turned their weapons in another direction, after that, and I heard this from my colleagues, a large number of people were taken to that centre, so at that point in time I didn't know what its status was. All I knew was one thing, and that is that it would be up to us to go and see what was going on there and what it looked like, but nobody gave me instructions to do that. However, when we arrived there, we found people there who, among other things, were medical technicians, some of them doctors, who were also incarcerated as HVO members. They were there and incarcerated because of those events, and we learnt that our own doctors from the brigade that was there in that compound were supervising, as much as they possibly could, healthcare for the centre. And then later on, we provided support, and I'll tell you how we did that. We provided support to the doctors in the centre and the doctors outside the centre who helped those inside it. So that would be more or less my answer to your question, but you must remember that it was July, the beginning of July, fairly early on, so at that point in time I couldn't have known this or that. It was just a place where I felt I needed to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bagaric, you said that you knew that within the frameworks of the barracks at Heliodrom there was a central prison, a central military prison?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, could you explain to Their Honours whether you visited that building of the Central Military Prison when you went with Mr. Lang or some other premises where there were detainees?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say -- I have to admit that now that you're asking me, I can't really say, I don't know whether we were here or there. But according to the people who were incarcerated there, looking at their ages and the situation that prevailed there in general, I think that -- well, I assume that it was a facility where people were placed who were incarcerated after the disarming of the BH Army, that is to say, those who were considered to be potentially dangerous at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, did you go to something that looked like a sports hall, a gymnasium, a gym hall?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not only do I think so, but, yes, I'm convinced that must have been it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now, from the reports and orders dating to July 1993 and ranging to the beginning of 1994, we see -- well, these reports were from Mr. Curic or the Infectology and Epidemiology Service, and you too. Now, my question is this: Would you say that as time went by, did the health situation improve? Because you said that you were in charge of healthcare as well, so did the situation improve, health protection situation improve, after you pointed out the negative aspects?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After our intervention, let me put it this way, our intervention from outside, and our assistance to the medical personnel inside and the people outside who supervised their work, we absolutely did promote [as interpreted] healthcare and protection in that area on the premises, but you must bear in mind that once again as time went by greater efforts were needed because the longer the people spent time in that place or in one particular place, there was the threat of infectious diseases breaking out, so that Dr. Curic, who later on became a coordinator - he's an infectologist and he came from outside - so he did more and more as time went on to deal with the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now let's look at some documents which relate to that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Nozica. Your question has not been answered. You asked whether the situation improved, and you -- Mr. Bagaric, yes, you say, "Yes," now, but generally I think you have mainly said that you continued your efforts and that it was more difficult, and it seems that you successfully prevented epidemics. Can you say in what other way the situation of the inmates was actually improved? I'm sorry, Ms. Tomanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for intervening. I believe that your question arises from the mistake in transcript. On page 19, line 6, it says here "we absolutely did promote," and what the witness actually said was "we absolutely did improve."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I said. I believe that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Lost in translation, as Mr. Karnavas would quote, and that's exactly the word which triggered off my question. Thank you. I think we can let Ms. Nozica go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am guilty because -- because I'm so fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, then slow down a little. We'll bear with you, and we'll tell you, we'll tell you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm doing my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, one question leading to another. I'm struck by the fact that you are talking about Dr. Curic for questions of epidemics. From a medical point of view, you're perfectly right, but you know that as regards the conditions of the inmates, there's only -- not only the problem of the epidemics, there are other issues; for example, the morale of the inmates, the overall detention conditions, the abuses, where doctors may have an extra role added on to that of taking care of infections or epidemics, and you're not talking about those aspects.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that I would be given time to talk about it at great length, that I would be given time. I understand your question. However, I can see that the counsel wants to speed things along, and that's why I am also rushing through my answers. And if you agree, if you want to hear my answers, I would very much like to provide them if there is time. Maybe I can do it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please rest assured, when Judges ask questions, this doesn't encroach on the time granted to the counsel. So answer my question and this will not be deducted from Ms. Nozica's time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're absolutely right, it was not just the concern about infections, but if you are looking after somebody, you have to carry out the overall role of monitoring and promotion of healthcare or improvement of healthcare, just like you said it. Our colleague, Dr. Curic, was the head of prevention and medical care, and believe me that he was a professional and he did everything as things should have been done, and you can tell by his reports that this was done professionally. What does this mean? At his proposal, we established a point, a medical point within the prison, which means that there was a doctor on duty there who examined people. He wore a white medical coat, and he treated people regularly, those who needed treatment, as this is normally done in any health centre anywhere. In addition to that, we also established a small warehouse with medical supplies and medicines there, so one could intervene very quickly if a need arose. And in those cases which could not be helped at that level, those people were brought to the Mostar Hospital. Mr. -- or the gentleman who was the head of the -- or the chief administrator of the Mostar Hospital was directly in charge of that. I would intervene from time to time should a problem have arisen in the communication. You have to bear in mind that Heliodrom was in the zone where operations -- where war operations were taking place, and it was not always easy to establish communication between the hospital and the Heliodrom, as such. And when you're talking about Mr. Curic, you mentioned his name, I believe -- I didn't understand, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I believe that the Judge said "Curic." We don't want to introduce any new names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was confused by that. I didn't understand. Can I continue, please, may I go on? Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: As there is an interruption, on page 21, line 19, it says that this medical point is normally done in any health centre anywhere. I wonder whether you actually said and wanted to say "health centre ," because I thought we were more appropriately talking about the prison, a detention centre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, correct. I would like to see the document. I don't know what document that is, but I know that that was indeed the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first thing that we did was to give importance to the doctors who, themselves, were detainees within the centre and the rest of the medical personnel. That is why I issued an order -- or, rather, it was a request. I don't know what it was, actually. It was a request to establish that centre and to be run by our colleagues, doctors who were detainees in the centre. In a certain way, we kept communication with them, with a constant supervision of their work from the outside, and that was taking place at two levels. The first level were the doctors who were in charge of the healthcare in that military district, and the other level was a higher professional level represented by Dr. Curic and other people who were with him from time to time and went there with him every now and then. Another thing that should be underlined here: As time went by, the situation there changed gradually, and every now and then we had to undertake some new activities, which you can see in the reports. However, one issue that you raised is something that I would like to go back to. You said that the environment, the surroundings in which people live, and the circumstances of their life, have a huge bearing on their health, which is absolutely correct, but we invested a lot of effort, and that effort resulted in the effects -- positive effects, that is, in the centre. Nobody suffered any harm. Everybody was treated medically. Of course, there were circumstances outside of the centre that had a direct impact on the health condition of the people in the centre that had nothing to do with the medical profession. For example, this could be the quality of their diet. It could be the safety of the detainees in the centre. And this is all true, and this compounded the matter even further, and it had an additional impact on the work of the doctors, making their life so much harder. There was an extent to which we could intervene, but there were also things that we could propose, and when I say "we," I mean the doctors directly in charge, but we did not have a bearing upon such things. All those things that we were trying to deal with had a lot of influence on the health of the people there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And, Mr. Bagaric, when I reach the documents, I was going to talk about them. This is very important, I would never have skipped that. However, I'm very glad that you did it in the Trial Chamber's time. Could you now please look at two or three very brief documents that have already been presented in the courtroom. The first one is 2D915. This should be the following document. It's a report on the sanitary -- supervision of the brigade Petar Kresimir IV. Could you look at the report and could you please confirm that this was indeed of the activities that was preformed by Dr. Curic, i.e., that was preformed by the Department for Infections, Epidemiology, and Toxicology? You said that you toured the brigade. Could you please confirm?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an example, one example -- a good example. Dr. Curic toured the brigade. He supervised the water supply. He made a note of the health conditions, and he, in doing that, established contact with the doctor who was in charge of the brigade. He also controlled whether the disease infection -- disease -- and all the other measures were carried out appropriately, whether there were health education measures in place, whether there was an active screening for infectious diseases, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, we have already heard a witness who testified about that. I would just like to ask you whether this could be a confirmation of what you've just been talking about.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The next document would be 2D2921 [as interpreted], which consists of two reports. The one is about the sanitary supervision of the Sup Vrdi [phoen] Sector, and after that is the report of the education in war prevention medicine. A doctor from the brigade in the locality Grude is being educated. Would this also fall under --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I apologise. The number has not been recorded properly. 2D921. My question has not been recorded properly. Did this fall under --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and the counsel please not overlap, because they cannot be interpreted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We've been warned, Witness, that you should wait for my question to end before you start providing your answer. Could you please look at P4756. This is a meeting of the collegium, and you said that one such meeting dealt with the detention centres. This was on 2nd of September, 1993. On page 3 in the Croatian and on page 4 in the English version of this document, you can see a record of the debate which took place at that meeting. Mr. Stojic said that he believed that the Defence Department had two military prisons, Heliodrom and Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You will provide a complete answer after my question. A task is given to check what was going on within a certain dead-line and to say who was behind the Dretelj and Gabela prisons and what was going on there. Can you remember whether the Health Department Sector also supervised the conditions in the latter two detention centres before and after this date?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is connected with the Presiding Judge's question about my knowledge or lack thereof on the status of the detention centres and prisons. I was really at that meeting of the collegium, and I know that things transpired exactly as they are recorded in here. However, I would like to emphasise that independently of all this, which I did not feel that Dretelj or Gabela were directly or charged, they indeed were not; however, by virtue of the same actions and responsibilities which governed us to supervise all the detention centres where infections could break out, I know that Dr. Curic, together with the doctors from the units that was in charge of the two detention centres, would enter those centres before and also later.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's now talk about some documents that speak about these two detention centres. Some have already been entered into evidence, so they will not call for your lengthy comments. The first document is P1415. This is your request dated 12th of August that you have already commented upon. Is this indeed the request in which you asked for a medical point to be set up in Heliodrom, as you have explained to the honourable Judge?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a document that I've already referred to. I was referring to an infantry point. This was our additional effort in order to deal with the problem and try and resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please look at the following document, which is 2D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, perhaps we could spare time by giving care to the numbers, because again this is a number which is not the correct one. The correct number is 041545, and you said "1415."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't think that any of us are right. The document number is P4145.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My colleague made a mistake. Everyone makes mistakes with figures; also I do. Witness, in this document there is something particular. I'd like you to explain this to me, because it's quite a feat to talk about a document you signed 15 years ago. The doctors of the 15th Brigade need to send somebody to take over the Heliodrom, and I'll repeat the question. In this document, it is stated that the doctors of the 2nd Brigade will be discharged at the Heliodrom. Why is this stated in that document? The 3rd Brigade and not 2nd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After having inspected the situation over there, and after having received the proposal from the doctor, Mirsad Stranjak, from the detention centre itself, and from Dr. Musa --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hold on. There was no French interpretation. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I don't speak French. I can't help you. Dr. Mirsad Stranjak, my colleague, the doctor who was within the detention camp, and Dr. Musa --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hold on. There is a problem because I cannot hear the French booth anymore. [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague, Mr. Mirsad Stranjak, who was in the centre itself as a detainee, and Dr. Musa, who was in the 3rd Brigade, who until then covered the centre or prison from outside with Dr. Curic, they in fact proposed that maximum autonomy be given to the doctors within the centre, and they said these people were important because they were doctors, because they had detention status, because the people who were with them had greater trust in them, if I can put it that way. They were more -- had more confidence in them. And so this person from the 3rd Brigade couldn't leave and not be interested in what the situation was like anymore there. No, that's not what the case was. But he didn't have to be there regularly, and this was reflected in the reports. He continued to visit from time to time and follow the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now let's look at 2D715, the next document, please. And this is an order from you. This is the first time you issue an order or command, and were you in a position to do so, to issue orders and commands? But we'll discuss that in a while. The date is the 18th of August, so let's see who it was addressed to. It says the command of the Knez Domagoj Brigade, to the attention of Colonel Nedeljko Obradovic, to the attention of Nikica Sutalo, and it relates to setting up a medical station, as it says herein, Dretelj Prison; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, so this is almost the identical situation here, and the way in which the problem at Heliodrom was solved, they tried to do the same here with Mr. Sutalo and Mr. Curic, and I'm sure he prepared this order. I did not sign it. I can see that somebody signed for me, because it's not my handwriting, but -- yes, I apologise for speaking so fast. I'll try and slow down. Anyway, as I was saying, I didn't sign this myself, but that's how things were. That was the rule. We had the authority to sign for each other, and so of course that was with my knowledge and agreement, and this meant entrance from outside, if I can put it that way, by a higher level of control and supervision going into Dretelj. And there you have it. The same principle applied.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now look at the next document, which is 2D278.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And it is an order signed by Mr. Curic this time, dated the 28th of August, and it followed on from, as it says here in the introduction, an investigation conducted on August the 17th, 18th, and 26th, and it was sent to the chief of the Health Service, Mr. Sutalo, and to Colonel Nedeljko Obradovic, and this is once again linked to an investigation of Gabela and Dretelj; right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here we can see the process was continuous, that people visited on the 17th, 18th, or maybe 19th, or 26th of August, and then there was a proposal made on the 28th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now let's look at 2D412, please, the next document. For the transcript, I have to repeat the number of the document. It is 2D412.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is an order from you, dated the 28th of September, and I think that it is repeated later on, but could you explain to Their Honours, please, what prompted you to issue an order like this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During your time or during the Judges' time?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, in my time, concisely, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very important order, and I'm very proud of this order, and I know that it led to quite a lot of success on the ground and that the situation was significantly improved, following the health of the detainees. We know that the circumstances and the situation was difficult, but quite certainly this order, together with the doctors who were inside and those who were outside, and especially with the help of my colleague Mr. Curic as an expert from outside at a higher level, this contributed to the significant promotion of healthcare in the premises. So this -- this applied to everything; what we knew about, and what we didn't know about. And if there had been a detention centre that we did not know about, it would nevertheless have made it incumbent upon the commanders to do their best to act.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you to look at P553, the next document. It is a report by the commission and it deals with a visit to the Heliodrom. On the 30th of September, and I think that this is important, to stress the date, linked to what Judge Antonetti asked you with respect to your request, P4145, the other document we saw a moment ago, I think it's important to say here that in addition to the three-member commission of doctors, that on behalf of the centre there was Mr. Stanko Bozic, the head of the centre, and Drs. Pehar [Realtime transcript read in error "Behar"] and Hadzic, and can you explain to Their Honours who Dr. Pehar was and who Dr. Hadzic was at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Pehar was the head -- well, I can't say whether he was the head of the brigade or the military district. I think he was the head of the brigade. Dr. Hadzic was a physician within the centre, and he was incarcerated. And as for this three-member commission, they are all doctors, specialists. Dr. Kolak was a surgeon. Well, he wasn't a surgeon at that time. He was just finishing his specialisation course. Then there was Dr. Ivo Sandrk, he was a specialist in general medicine. And Ivo Sturic [phoen], whom I've already said was an infectologist. So all three of them were the heads of certain departments within our Health Sector. So this was -- well, Curic as a professional, he supervised the situation himself, but in order to have a more comprehensive and all-embracing approach, these two other doctors were added to the commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let me repeat the number of the document. The document we've just been commenting upon is P5503, 5503. I'm saying that for the record, Witness, and I'm now going to ask you to look at two more documents. They are both reports, and let me just draw your attention to the fact that on page 31, line 8, it should read "Dr. Pehar" with a "P" instead of "Behar" with a "B." Could you look at 2D1538 next, please. We saw from your order, especially the order from the 28th of August, where you ask that reports be submitted to you -- the document number is 2D1538.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm saying that for the record. Now, can you tell us whether this is one such report that followed after the inspection took place?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is one of the reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a response to Mr. Nikica Sutalo, linked to the Centre for Preventive Isolation, Gabela, and I'd like to draw your attention to the last sentence. It says there are no difficulties in the centre's operation with regards to the medical aspect; is that right? So you received reports like this from other centres for preventive isolation as well; right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my answer is "yes," but I can't remember all the details now because Dr. Curic, in a way and conditionally speaking, was appointed by us. Well, we reached an agreement to appoint him to be in charge of supervision from outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Bagaric, look at a report like that dated the 15th of January, 1993. It is 2D1537.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm still a bit confused about the last document. You have said - this is line 8, page 32 - "This is a response to Mr. Nikica Sutalo," but it seems that it is a document signed by Nikica Sutalo. So if it is a response, it will not be an auto-response of him to himself?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're quite right. It's not to Nikica Sutalo, it's from Nikica Sutalo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Right. And it would be very interesting -- maybe you could tell us, Dr. Bagaric, what was the position of Dr. Sutalo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, I think my colleague Mr. Sutalo was the head of the Medical Corps of the Knez Domagoj Brigade, that's what I think he was, and that's how he signs himself here, head of the Sanitary Service or Medical Corps, SNSL.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And was he also the person responsible for the medical aspects in Gabela?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely so, yes, he was one of the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So this is not a report by someone who is outside and goes to see whether the previous order has been complied with, but it's the person to whom the order was addressed who said, I did everything you asked me for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question to ask. Ms. Nozica, you still have seven minutes, and while I'm asking my question, see how you are going to use the seven minutes with the few documents you still have. Witness, I just had a look at the two reports of Dr. Sutalo, and I see -- I notice this, and the first document, Dr. Sutalo reports on the situation of the centre, isolation centre, Preventive Isolation Centre, that's how it's titled, and the second report in November, the title given is "Report on the Situation of the Measures Made at the Prison Gabela." Therefore, in a few weeks, within the span of a few weeks, this isolation centre of preventive medicine becomes a prison. And so I know that Dr. Sutalo is not a lawyer, but could you give an explanation? Do you have any explanation to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not a lawyer. But tell me, what was the second document? I see the first one, but what's the second, just for me to compare?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was number 2D1538, and the second document is 2D1537.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see. This is a typical -- the typical kind of report that doctors would write in which Dr. Dr. Sutalo, at least that's how I see it, he puts "Subject: Report on the Situation in the Centre for Preventive Isolation, Gabela," that's what he put as a subject, and this other one, the report on the current situation in Gabela Prison and the measures taken. Now, I don't know whether the status of that centre changed at all, but it wouldn't be unusual had Dr. Sutalo meant the same thing, using both these titles, because I've already said that at that time, even as far as terminology is concerned, we didn't know how to call things by their right name, but what is essential is that people were there. That's the main point.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Might I be of assistance to Judge Trechsel, when he asked who Nikica Sutalo was, I thought that -- let me just remind you of 2D715, that document, and 2D -- 2D715, we've already looked at that document, at 2D278, which is -- one is an order from Mr. Bagaric which was directly sent to Mr. Nikica Sutalo, and the second was an order Mr. Curic, which was addressed to Nikica Sutalo, and his position is stated there, head of the Medical Corps. It says that it is the Knez Domagoj Brigade at the top.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've just said that. I apologise for saying that, Counsel, but I said --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, just take it easy. No need to get upset. I see that you have a rather feisty temperament, but take things slowly, just one by one. Now let's look at the next document. May I have just a minute or two more time, Your Honours, and I'm sure I'll be over by the break. But let's look at P6203 now, please. P6203 is the number.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a document written to -- coming to you from Mr. Siljeg, concerning a letter of yours from the 28th of October, unfortunately an order that we don't have. But, anyway, he says, first of all, that as far as the centres are concerned, or the ones on his territory, that there aren't any, but I'm interested under B where he says: "You do not have the right to command," to issue orders, and that makes your orders null and void. Do you have any comments there, whether Mr. Siljeg, at least in formal terms -- well, did you have the right to issue commands, and may we have your comments?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I couldn't issue orders to him, and I didn't do that either, but I think what is more important here is what we wanted to achieve and what we did achieve. That's more important than how -- what we call the document. That was immaterial.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you have any military training of any kind, you and Mr. Stojic and the Defence Department, so that you would know how documents should be written, what a command is, what an order is, what an instruction is or whatever?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Siljeg, who came from the Yugoslav People's Army and was a well-educated and trained soldier, knew the terminology better than me. I was somebody who did not have this basic formal military training, so I might have called things by a different name. But let me repeat once again, that was unimportant.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now the last document that we're going to look at is P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We leave aside your view on what is important and what is not, but I would like to ask you: You could not, of course, give an order to Colonel Obradovic, that's for sure, but could you not give an order to the medical staff which was attached to Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have said that this was not important. This order that I termed "order" and to which Siljeg protested actually had not been addressed to Siljeg, but his assistant for healthcare. His assistant for healthcare in the hierarchy chain, obviously he was under the command of Mr. Siljeg. However, in the professional sense, I believe that I could issue a document and call it an order. I agree with you, it was my personal belief that I was in a position to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: P5035 is the next document, a report by the Spanish delegation. I'm going to show you just some excerpts that you already saw in the proofing session. Item 5 of this report refers to the hospital in West Mostar. It says that the hospital was under construction for ten years. Over the past 18 months, they had about 6.000 seriously wounded that they operated on. It has problems with the supply of water and electricity. They don't have all the necessary medicines. In addition to that, they also need more adequate medical equipment. The doctors complain that they get help only from foreign religious organisations, but were receiving barely any support from the International Red Cross and the UNHCR. And now on the following page, we have all the problems that you pointed out with regard to the situation in Nova Bila, problems with the International Red Cross. You repeat that you have proposed --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I am repeating that. He says that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that in the conversation that you had with him, you repeated that, as you had so many times, under 7 is the visit to the Detention Centre Heliodrom, and it says here the conditions are poor; however, it seems that the detainees are rather well fed and accommodated, and the detainees themselves had installed central heating. This was on the 14th of September, 1993, when this document was drafted. They had running water 24 hours a day, and they have plenty of toilets and bathrooms. Since the Heliodrom is normally barracks, there is a system of ventilation. The detainees were registered by the International Red Cross. There are two outpatient clinics, with one doctor each and a few nurses. There are no health problems: "When we asked the detainees about food, they told us that they were receiving two meals a day, and the warden said that they were receiving three meals a day. The detainees where wearing normal civilian clothes, and they were obliged to work in the camp." I'm now going to ask you to try and compare this with item 10, which describes the detention centre in East Mostar. This detention centre is in the cellar of a civilian building. It does not have a system of ventilation, to speak of. There is just one bulb. The light was poor. All the detainees wore prison clothes, and they had just returned from work. They looked at -- rather terrified, and they didn't want to speak in the presence of their guards: "Still, we did receive some information from them. They confirmed that they had received one meal a day, plenty of water, and that they had to do all sorts of jobs and dig trenches. They said that they had not been visited by any representatives of the International Red Cross and that they had not been given an opportunity to send messages to the International Red Cross." And the last sentence in this report says: "The conditions of life of the detainees on the east side are much worse than the conditions on the west bank at Heliodrom and can be described as really sad." Mr. Bagaric, I have left this document for the end of your examination-in-chief. This confirms what you told us, and that is that once you invested effort, the health conditions improved. Does this report improve [as interpreted] that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How much time do I have?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You tell me.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does confirm that. It's, in a certain way, an objective picture of the situation. He mentions two outpatient clinics, doctors, which were all the result of our efforts that we invested together with the inmates who were doctors. Therefore, it is obvious that the Muslim Bosniak side worked against my wishes, but that was not a reason for us not to do our utmost in order to provide healthcare for the people who were there. I believe that this is a good confirmation of everything; maybe not everything, but at least that part that I was talking about and that concerned the life in the prisons.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My last question, Mr. Bagaric: You personally were engaged in the Health Department, and you were also engaged when it came to the assistance to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You tried to help them in medical equipment and the supplies. Did you enjoy Mr. Stojic's support in all that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that - and I have to be honest here, and I promised I would be sincere - that it was not every time, although this probably wasn't fair, that I did not ask Mr. Stojic's support every time for this or that. However, I enjoyed that support in absolute terms, and I believe that I had a carte blanche for my efforts, and I behaved in accordance with that, even in such situations when I was not in charge of the things directly. However, I felt that an additional intervention was required, that an additional pressure was needed for the things to be put in motion and improved under the conditions from hell. If I may add to that one more sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were engaged in that operation together with Sally Backer, I don't know how else would have we been able to do it if we would not have Mr. Stojic's support and the support of General Praljak who was at the time I don't know what. He was the commander of the whole area, I believe. And so what was needed was a cease-fire for -- at least on our side, for this evacuation to be successful. And this is the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you, Your Honours. This brings my examination-in-chief to an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we have a break, the Judges would like to know the intention of counsels for cross-examination. I'll proceed very quickly. Of the three counsels, are there going to be any questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, we do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We also have some questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D5. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as things stand now, we won't have any questions. However, this is not our final word.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we will probably not examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, Mr. President. Good afternoon, sir, and good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. We will not have any questions. However, we have yielded our time to the Praljak Defence. But we do wish to take this opportunity to thank the gentleman for coming here to give his evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. During the break, D3 and D4 will calculate their time, and D5 as well, if necessary. Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. I give the floor to the first counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good afternoon. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, good afternoon to you too.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, we know each other, don't we?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You will also be a Defence witness for General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: For the time being, we have agreed that you will testify about the meeting that you mentioned in Jablanica at the beginning of May 1993, of your departure to Sovici, and the inspection of the Jablanica and Konjic regions, and your attempts to calm the tensions, to evacuate the wounded, and to establish a normal situation there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, we met last Sunday, in the evening; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And we spent some two hours in a conversation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether we discussed the documents that Mr. Stojic's Defence prepared for your examination-in-chief or did we discuss other topics?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we discussed any documents at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. I'm going to ask you several questions with regard to your testimony so far. The first group of questions will deal with the organisation of healthcare in military units. And I believe that so far you have been very fair in interpreting the decisions on the internal establishment and formation of the military units, but I believe that some things have not been placed well in time. So I will need some clarification. I'm going to ask you about your meeting in Sarajevo towards the end of August 1993 and the agreement that was reached between Delic and Petkovic with regard to the evacuation of the wounded. You said that you attended that meeting, so I'm going to have some questions for you with this regard. I'm also going to ask you several questions about the detention centres, and primarily those that arise from your answers provided earlier today, and I will particularly ask you to clarify an answer of yours which I believe is very important. And if we still have the time left, I'm going to ask you just one question about your answer with regard to the inspection of Sovici, although this is going to be the main topic of your testimony in the Petkovic case. And I'm going to ask that question, because I promised my learned friend Scott that I would ask that question, because it was provoked by his reaction to one of your answers about the alleged crimes that were either committed or not committed in Sovici. Let's start with first things first, and that is healthcare in military units. First of all, Dr. Bagaric, I'm going to try and sum up what you told us yesterday and what is going to be the main topic of my questions. This is recorded on page 21 of yesterday's transcript. Dr. Bagaric, if I'm not mistaken, you said that the Healthcare Sector in the Defence Department organised and coordinated the work of medical personnel in the military units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can put it that way, but this is not the whole answer. But, yes, you can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You will have an opportunity to clarify further. You said, amongst other things, that the objective of the organisation of healthcare was to take the healthcare from the Logistics Sector?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And to provide healthcare professionals in the military units with the status of assistant commanders?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was our intention. However, I must admit that we did not succeed completely. There were places when this was carried through, but there were also others where this did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You've said that the success depended on the commander of the military units, so you were successful at places and at others you were not. Would that sum up your yesterday's testimony fairly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at my binder of documents. We will take each of them at a time, one by one. We have the first document, which is 2D567 or 2D00567.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is a decision on the internal organisation of the Defence Department. Please look at the last page of the document and tell us, please, Dr. Bagaric, who was authorised to issue such a decision? Who issued this decision, actually?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember this specific document. However, according to what I see here, I can see who signed the decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It arises from the signature this decision was issued by the head of the Defence Department, with the agreement of the president of the HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the document, that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Under item 5 that you spoke about yesterday, and this item deals with the Medical Sector, a reference is made to the chief of medical care of the brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would it be fair to conclude that that health professional did not enjoy the status of assistant brigade commander, but rather that he was the chief of a medical corps?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't infer this, either one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at item 4, dealing with the Security Sector, and also look at the bullet point 3.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, bear with me. I have to find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It's one page before. It says here: "Assistant commander for security in operative zone commands are appointed by the head of the Defence Department ..." And I skip the rest. And it says further: "On assistant commanders for security are appointed by the head of the Defence Department," and so on and so forth. Tell me, please, would it arise from this that the commanders of operative zones and brigades had assistants for security?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you - please don't hold it against me. If I don't have to, I would not answer questions about security, because I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm not you, Dr. Bagaric, about security. I'm just trying to show you that this decision that we are talking about right now establishes who the assistant of commanders of the operative zone or brigades are, and I'm trying to tell you that this is prescribed by the Security Sector, that this is prescribed by the Sector for Morale and Education, which is under item 6, and this does not exist in the Health Sector area, and hence my question: Does this mean that this decision did not provide for the commanders of operative zones and brigades to have assistants for healthcare; it is only prescribed that they will be chief of the Medical Corps?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So what was the situation like?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Actually, not that I don't know; I can tell you what it says here and what it doesn't say here. I can only tell you how it was in practice in real life and how we functioned. I really can't tell you what would happen if something else had happened. I apologise for this answer of mine. I really don't understand this type of conversation. Does this mean that this was the case and the other thing was not the case? I really can't follow you. I don't understand you. I can tell you how it looked like in practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, I'm asking you about this decision because you only spoke about this decision in the examination-in-chief by the Stojic Defence, and I'm going to be going through the exact same documents with you. I'm going to show you the next document, which is the next one in the series, which is P02477, 2477, and this is another decision on the internal organisation of the Defence Department, dated 20 May 1993. Please look at the item 5, and again the reference is made only to the chief of the medical corps brigade.
