Can we agree at least on one thing, Dr. Bagaric, and that is that this decision does not mention the assistant commander for healthcare? Can we agree at least on that? Is there any doubt about that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at this document, then, you will see that a reference is made to the chief of the brigade medical corps. However, you cannot see -- it does not transpire from this document what his position was within the brigade. In other words, it doesn't say here that he was an assistant commander, but this is not conclusive. You can't say that he wasn't, because there were other documents that could have regulated this, and they indeed did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Since you were a military professional, would you say that the position of a chief of a -- of the chief of a service, and, on the one hand, and the position of the assistant commander are completely the same positions or not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you then agree that in this decision there is no single reference to the operational zones and the medical service in the operation zones?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There could be a confusion. I'm trying to shed some light on this. A doctor in a military unit, what is his main role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His main role is to monitor the health situation in the unit. And if that unit is engaged in combat, then he has to determine the routes for evacuation of the wounded, establish the points for reception, and to establish the service so that it could function in the field on the strength of the unit and follow its war path.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Now, coming back to Ms. Alaburic's question as to why the brigade commander doesn't have a deputy or an assistant, is it because the doctor has a specific role, which is to provide treatment, which means that he's not in the front-line for military operations like the assistant for security or propaganda would be, which would account for the fact that the doctor, like the imam or the Catholic priest in the unit, has a specific -- a particular position in the unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand you, Your Honour. However, I believe that here, in this concrete case, when I analyse this, I must admit that I don't remember this document at the time when it was drafted. However, there is an evident error that was made in this document here. The chief of the brigade medical corps is mistakenly incorporated into this document, and let me tell you why. Here a reference is made to the Healthcare Sector, the Healthcare Sector, and when you're talking about the Healthcare Sector in this document, then you exclusively refer to the segment over which I was in direct command, and I'm talking about the 25 or 30 men that I was in charge of, and there were three basic elements there. One of them was the service for the care of the wounded, the chief of the Medical Corps, and the chief of the Control and Inspection Service. In other words, war hospitals are a separate story, and I can understand that they are here. However, the chief of the medical corps of the brigade, this is a pure mistake, a pure nonsense that I probably did not see at the time. If I had seen it, I would have intervened, because this is nonsense. How can you have a chief of the brigade medical corps if that person was in his unit? On the other hand, Ms. Alaburic is right in the part where she says that there should also be the main person for healthcare at the level of a military district. This is actually the proof that the chief of the medical corps of the brigade has found himself here by mistake. And if this was my proposal at the time, then I made a mistake, but I don't think so. I really don't know how this ended up here, because it's a -- it's a sheer nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, in my questions I'm not trying to -- I'm not trying to entrap you by my questions.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not setting a trap for you either.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the following document that the Defence of Bruno Stojic showed you. This is document number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, I would like to come back to your last question and the issue of assistant commander. If you look at the original text of the last subparagraph of Chapter C, like in "Caesar," they speak of "bomocnik prestonika," [phoen], and then there is the "prestonik" [phoen] himself mentioned. Now, "bomocnik prestonika," is that not something like assistant commander, assistant to the commander?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I would like to say this: In the second paragraph of item number 5, it says that the assistant to the head of the Health Department, Dr. Bagaric, will appoint all the other officials and operatives for healthcare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I have to explain. It's not true, this is not correct. May I? May I be given the leave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I am in document 2477, number 5, paragraph 2. I do not see any reference to any person appointing someone?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, microphone: "All of the employees and operatives are assigned by this assistant head for medical services with previous approval of the head of the Defence Department or a person authorised by him," which means --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Which means that I was somewhat mistaken. Thank you for enlightening me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to come back to this. I have to explain for the Trial Chamber to understand, because I'm finding it difficult to understand it. And I appreciate that it must be even more difficult for you, who have never served in the army. Will you allow me, please? Under item 5, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're all in the army, so don't say that the Judges were never in the army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not say that. I said "in our army." In the army, that was rather complicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second paragraph of item 5 -- and I believe that the counsel has been mistaken because of the wording of this particular paragraph. It says here all the other employees and operatives are assigned by the assistant head for Medical Services, which was myself, I was the assistant head for Medical Services, with previous approval of the head of the Defence Department, but this refers to my -- yesterday's Healthcare Sector, because that's what my small unit was called, and that unit was a unit within the Defence Department. It was my Healthcare Sector, and I was the one who assigned those people and proposed those people. And I am talking about 25 to 30 people altogether, not all the people in Healthcare Services. There was no way I could appoint somebody in Central Bosnia whom I didn't know, with whom I did not have any contact, and I didn't know who the local commander over there appointed as a doctor. It would be pointless. How could I, as a doctor, be in command? I, from the headquarters, how could I be in command over a doctor who was serving in the hills, engaged in combat? That would be totally insane. I've already told you several times that our organisation was not perfect, but there was still some sort of organisation. So that's the mistake. This is what I'm trying to tell you, and as soon as you understand this, we'll be able to be on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We are on the same page, Mr. Bagaric, but let's move on along the documents. Could you please look at 2D927, which is a document that was issued by Mr. Bruno Stojic, and this is the establishment of the command of the operative zone. You already commented on this yesterday, and we dealt with bullet point 30 of this document. And you clarified for us, if I understood properly your conversation with my learned friend Nozica, that this is about the chief of Medical Care Services.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are we talking about? Are we talking about the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is the operation zone.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the operation zone, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I can see that you're talking at the same time. You must make an effort to be a bit slower and to expect to -- to wait a while after the question has been put, because it first has to be translated. This is very demanding, it's really a tough exercise, but it is absolutely essential. I think you can proceed or resume a bit ahead, because ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, we can say that yesterday you confirmed to the Stojic Defence that under bullet point 30 is the position or the establishment position of the chief of the Medical Services, is that correct, within the operation zone?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "Medical Services," and what is missing here is an explanation. I don't know what it is. It says "Medical Services" here, but I assume that since there's just one professional, that this refers to the doctor who is in charge of medical services in the military zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Look at bullet point 26, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat what I said for the record, and let's take it slowly. Look at point 26. You say: "Assistant to the commander for logistics." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, Mr. Bagaric, knowing documents of this kind, does it follow that the head of the Medical Corps was in that Department for Logistics or, rather, that he was subordinate to the assistant to the commander for logistics?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't understand it that way, because he's at place 30, whereas this man for logistics is in the 26th place. I don't think that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now take a look at the next document, which is 2D1370, which is the brigade formation plan. And it's a document that you discussed yesterday with Ms. Nozica, if you remember. Now take a look at the following. Well, you discussed the positions on page 4 of the Croatian and page 6 of the English, under number 8, where it says: "Chief of Medical Service." Can you confirm, Dr. Bagaric, that that is how it was or was yesterday? Is that what we said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What formation did this refer to?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The brigade.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it should be as the chief of the Medical Service.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now turn over the page to see what department that belongs to. And it would appear that the Logistics Department, among other things, has under its composition a chief of a medical service, and tell me, does that follow from this document, Dr. Bagaric? Does it follow from the document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. I'll tell you. That is what follows from this document. However, I don't know who compiled this plan, so it wasn't important, as far as I was concerned, that it should be put down on paper in one way or another. What was important was what would happen on the ground, in the field, and what the status would be. Would he be the assistant to the commander or some number 10 man in logistics? Do you see what I'm getting at, what I mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now take a look at document P566, please, which is the battalion formation plan or chart, and that's to be found on page 2. And if you look at the right-hand corner, you said that the Medical Department came under the composition of the Logistics Platoon or the medical squad was under the Logistics Platoon. Now, from this document, does that follow, that the medical corps or squad was under the Logistics Platoon?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What date is this document, what's the date of it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It's the 9th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, well, that's where the problem lies, that's the problem. Somebody compiled this as they thought it -- they drew it up according to what they thought it should look like on paper, but they forgot the fact. We established the Medical Corps before the brigade was formed at all, any brigade, before any brigade was set up. How did we do that? We set up the Main Medical Staff or headquarters, and then the chiefs of the different medical squads or corps, and we looked at the municipalities and who was the chief in the municipality medical centre. But looking at this piece of paper, you could understand it the way you've just explained.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: From your answers yesterday, I gathered that organisation for the health service in the military units of this kind was not very good, and that's why it needed to be reorganised. Did I understand you correctly, was my interpretation of what you said correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the part where I said that we doctors weren't satisfied with staying under logistics, and we tried to emerge from this logistics cocoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, then I did understand you correctly. I just wanted to offer up the following thesis: that the reorganisation was supposed to separate the Health Service from Logistics and put medical persons in the different units and in the operative zones; right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, the next document is 2D1540, and it is a document that you discussed yesterday. It is an order, Bruno Stojic, the 8th of October; that is to say, approximately a year after the documents we looked at a moment ago. It is an order from Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 8th of October, 1993, that is the order, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, in the introduction, it says that he is issuing the following command because of the problems with commanding and directing in HVO formations when it comes to wartime healthcare, and that the command is designed to resolve the situation that came into effect because as a result of irreverence of organisational structures of the military; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we analyse the first three points of this command or order or document, we'll see that there are certain functions which we did not have, at least not under those titles and names, in the documents that we have seen so far, and they are the chief of the operative zone for wartime healthcare, then the chief of the brigade's wartime healthcare, and the chief of the battalion's wartime healthcare; is that right, Mr. Bagaric -- Dr. Bagaric? These are new posts that we haven't seen yet in the documents we've looked at?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we haven't seen them in documents, but we did see them on the ground, in reality. In certain places, it was like this, and in others, it wasn't. And for it to be as is stipulated here, we called for the changes to be made, the restructuring, and that's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, does this command state that the chiefs of wartime healthcare will be the assistants to the commanders of the operative zone or brigade or, rather, battalion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, in essence, does this command change the decision on the establishment of Defence Department that we looked at a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which department do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The Health Sector of the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this order has nothing at all to do with the establishment we looked at a moment ago, and nothing changed in that establishment, but I still maintain that the brigade sort of lost its way and found its way there. How could a brigade not have a battalion? It's nonsensical.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Bagaric, you told us several times, and I'll quote you, that the report on the wounded could be compiled only by a physician because that kind of report would give a description of the wound. You told us about the professional medical duties involved. Now, could you tell us, what did the health workers, regardless of the military unit they were in, what did they have to do? Were they engaged in professional medical work? That's my first question, in fact.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. Of course what they did involved professional medical duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, what duties, apart from these professional medical duties, did they perform?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: Professional medical duties, that's one term, and it's seen differently in peacetime and wartime. In peacetime, it involves the profession and care of the sick, but professional medical duties during a war includes other things as well; ensuring the evacuation of the wounded, evacuation routes, and the technology of taking care of them in the field, which is something that doesn't have to be done during peacetime. So a doctor, a physician in a unit, was somebody who -- well, was a doctor, first and foremost, so performing his professional duties, but he was also a soldier. That is to say, his commander, his commanding officer, could say, for example, The unit is going to March off in such and such a direction. Provide medical security. So that would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, I didn't ask you about the contents of professional medical duties or what they entailed, but I asked you that apart from their professional medical duties, whatever those were, and regardless of whose orders they were under, did they have any other duties that weren't professional medical duties?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: For example, did they take any military decisions or decisions relating to security, or anything that doesn't come under medicine?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had to take many decisions that had nothing to do with their profession in peacetime, but in wartime of course they had something to do with their profession, they were linked to their vocational training. But, once again, I don't really see where you're getting -- see where you're going.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, which is 4D1326, and maybe things will become clearer. This is a chart which the Petkovic Defence prepared.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What number did you say?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: 4D1326. Davor Lazic, who is sitting next to me, compiled this on the basis of the document that we discussed a moment ago, 2D1540, and from that document we can see what is expounded in points 4, 5, and 6 of the order issued by Mr. Bruno Stojic. Let me correct the document number. 4D1326. Oh, I'm sorry, that's -- that was the right number. I'd like to correct the other number. The Stojic Defence document, on the basis of which the chart was compiled, is document 2D1540. Very well. Now, tell me, please, Dr. Bagaric, you know this Stojic document. You saw it during the proofing session, and in blue here we marked the military chain, where we see that the assistant for health was responsible to the commander, and the red line is the professional chain of reporting and responsibility, leading from the battalion, via the brigade and the operative zone, to the Health Sector. Now, Dr. Bagaric, could you tell us, please, whether this chart, in your opinion, is a correct reflection of what Bruno Stojic's order says, or is there something that is amiss in this chart?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This chart is an interpretation. Let me put it that way. What does professional responsibility mean at all? I see that this is a term that we don't see eye to eye on. There were doctors over there. Now, my sector, my Health Sector, my colleagues, they won't go and question and examine their professional qualifications. They are qualified because they're doctors, and so they have a certain duty to perform, and we can take it that they're doing their job properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, I do have the right to interrupt you, because I want to ask you the following question: The term "professional" is not something that I have thought up. The term "professional" is used in the Stojic document that you discussed yesterday, so please take a look at points 4, 5, and 6, where it says that the chief of wartime health in the professional aspect tables a report and is responsible to the chief of wartime healthcare and the Health Sector ultimately. So this term "professional," as far as I understood it yesterday --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me find the document. Ah, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, you told us yesterday that you, in fact, prepared a draft for -- the draft for this order.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you used the term "professional"?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. If I did use it and if I did compile it, then I'll explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait until counsel has finished the question before you answer, because there's an overlapping all the time. Witness, listen. This document is a source of confusion. Even for a Judge, there is a series of problems on the basis of this document. Let's take a concrete case to try and understand this situation. Imagine a doctor who works in a battalion, and the commander of the battalion tells him, At 6.00 a.m., we will attack the enemy defence, and therefore you have to come with us because there's a risk of having some wounded people, so we need your presence, you have to be there. In this case, the doctor will have -- will be obliged to obey because he's a military doctor, and therefore he's going to have to follow the unit. So what one sees in blue here, he's under the authority of the commander of the battalion who tells him to be present. But then when he is going to treat the wounded, that becomes his own responsibility. The commander of the battalion hasn't got to tell him -- will not tell him whether he should operate or give a transfusion. That becomes the responsibility of the medic. Would you be in agreement with what I've just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So with this example as presented by Ms. Alaburic, he seems to be under the authority of the commander of the battalion, but these red lines, he can come to you to say, This is the problem: We have three wounded. We need a helicopter, but there is no helicopter. So you have to make contact with ICCR [as interpreted] or the Spanish Battalion to solve the problem because we have a medical problem here. In this case, would it happen that way? How would it be solved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right. In a case like that, the doctor would first of all talk to his commander, military commander, that is, and the military commander would organise a helicopter flight. I can't organise a helicopter if I am far away, and I'm a doctor anyway. So I don't deal in logistics and can't order a helicopter to fly. So that's where the trick lies, if I can use the word. Now, if we're talking about some kind of professional terminology, I agree with counsel that this is really rather disconcerting, because it does say so on paper, all that does say so on paper, but things worked -- well, the Medical Sector should have worked in the field you way you described it, and that's how it was and that's what we wanted to achieve, which means that the chief of the Health Service or the number-one person in the unit is the assistant to the commander. Now, why? Because we have -- there were special circumstances. Our commanders were very often, especially those in the Logistics Centre, were uneducated people, whereas a doctor was a professional, he was a physician, educated, regardless of his military knowledge, and he would not have been able to act, he would not have been able to make decisions, if somebody who was a logistics man in the unit were to command him and be in charge of him. So we wanted to avoid this in order to allow us to function better, but I was not superior to him at all, in the sense of any of the activities that you mentioned, but only in the sense that, for example, when Dr. Curic, whom we mention fairly often here, goes out into the field and sees, for example, whether preventive medicine, preventive medical protection is being put in place, he could give guide-lines and instructions to the physician and even issue orders to improve the professional situation as a professional himself, so that's a good example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, concrete examples, please, because if we don't have them, nobody will understand anything anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me for just a minute. I would like to try and give an example, a practical example. Let's say, for instance, that the chief medic sees that the reserves and plaster supply are diminishing, so he asks to keep the plaster for broken legs, but not for broken arms. For arms, you'll have to find another means. Would this be an example of an order which could be sent by the red line which is indicated here? You have to answer verbally, because if you just move your head, there is nothing which says so in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a doctor in the unit was logistically relying on the logistical support on his own unit. If he needed dressing or anything else of this sort, then they were the ones who had to provide it. He did not have to concern himself with that. However, since our circumstances were very special and we did not have enough materials and medicines, then we, as the Main Medical Corps, before we were incorporated within the Defence Department, we had established our own warehouse where we stocked medicines from donations, so when we received a request from a doctor on the ground, we would help him as much as we could, because there was no medical logistics within the unit itself. And that, I hope, answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, could you please explain something. In answering Judge Antonetti's question, you have often said that you concluded that the things were not functioning, that you decided to reorganise things. When you say "we" in this case, who exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who do I mean? I mean doctors. From time to time, one of the doctors from my sector, the Healthcare Sector, inspected the area and would talk to the doctor in the field and hear from him certain objections to the prevalent conditions, and then in a certain way we would build our policy for the functioning of the service, but we never interfered with its operation. In general terms, we were able and we were in a position to institute some changes for the better. However, it was not on a daily basis that we communicated with every single doctor on the ground. It was impossible. It would have been pointless. No single military in the world does that, and it would have been totally pointless, nonsensical.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, again you're using the pronoun "we." Does this mean it is you professionals in the Healthcare Sector in the Defence Department; is that who you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only that. I said "us doctors." I'm talking about the whole profession, the whole medical profession, and I meant those who were in the field and us, because we did communicate from time to time, we did monitor the situation on the ground, and we adapted to the situation as much as we could in order to assist them as much as we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, I am asking you: Who had the authority to issue a decision to reorganise the Healthcare Service, who held that authority?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order for this to happen, this was primarily within the purview of the commander at the highest level of the military, and in our own case those were also chiefs of medical services of military districts, and of course we all participated in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, you have to explain one thing for me. Who were the commanders at the highest level of the military who had the authority to issue decisions on the organisation of the Healthcare Service in military units? I would ask you to tell us precisely the position or function. You can give us names, whatever you will, but please be very precise and tell us who it was.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said it. Those were the commanders of the war hospitals, the commanders -- what are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, I'm asking you very concretely about the organisation of the entire Healthcare Service, whether it will be part of the Ministry of Defence or whether it will be under the Main Staff, whether there will be a chief of the Medical Service, or whether the person will be the assistant commander of a unit. The complete organisation of healthcare, who was it who was authorised to decide on that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The formal authority to write something, as it says here and as you can see it here on the paper, it was the Ministry of Defence. That's where the formal authority lie. But this was prepared with the commander of the Main Staff, the commanders of the units, the doctors, the number-one persons, doctors. We have seen a decision which was not of that kind. This is what I've been telling you about. We still functioned I would say under specific circumstances, which is understandable, and it is not always that everything followed word on the paper. I understand what you're trying to say, but I am not willing to accept that, because that's not how things were, because -- and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What am I trying to say, Mr. Bagaric?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's put it this way: You are trying to convince me all this time that I, as the commander or, rather, the assistant head of the Defence Department [as interpreted] was the direct commander of every doctor in every unit, which is a nonsense. That's simply how it did not happen, and if somebody had pushed me into accepting that, I would not have accepted that because it's not normal. It would not have been normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, please tell me which of my questions, which of my remarks or anything that I've said has made you conclude that this is what I'm aiming at?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From everything that you have told me so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Dr. Bagaric, when you say that you were the number-one person in the healthcare of the HVO -- you said it several times earlier today. Do you remember, do you remember that you said it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, I'll accept that I've said it. However, this had a very special and symbolical meaning. What does it mean to be number-one person? That means to be the highest-position person, the person at the highest position with very concrete powers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I have just one more question for you dealing with this area. I've prepared a document that deals with the Croatian Army. This is 4D1427. I wanted to show you the diagram on page 2 both in Croatian and in English. It says here that it is within the purview of the chief of the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Croatia is also the Administration for Logistics, and on the following page there is a definition of everything that is under the Administration for Logistics, and it says here that that administration also contains healthcare. Based on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, Ms. Alaburic. I would like, Dr. Bagaric, that you would look at the last question [sic] you have given. You were asked: "Weren't you the number one?" And you said: "Okay, I'll accept that I've said it. However, this is a very special and symbolic meaning. What does it mean to be number-one person? That means to be the highest-position person, the person at the highest position, with very concrete powers." Now, what is missing, what is missing, is: Does that correspond to your position or were you explaining that you were not the man who had real power and who were really the boss? Were you the boss or were you not the boss? That's the question, put very, very primitively.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I was the highest-position doctor in the Ministry of Health, i.e., in the Defence Department, which was later on the Health Ministry. However, I was the highest position, and I accept with pride that I was person number one. But that doesn't mean that I was directly in command of the doctors and healthcare units in the field, which Ms. Alaburic is trying to imply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So I'm being a bit satirical, not -- I'm taking all this very seriously, but sometimes it's easier if someone makes bit drastic pictures. Mainly, what you had was the beautiful uniform and the nice hat, and everyone bowed to you, and you were made to enter the door before the others. But when it came to giving orders, to making other people do what you wanted them to do, you had not much of that kind of power. Is that what you are telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not that. Your Honour, I was the chief of the Main Medical Staff at the beginning, before the Defence Department was ever established and before the Defence Ministry were established. When they were established, I was the highest-position doctor and I assumed the position of the assistant head. And it is not true and I can't say that I did not have powers. However, my powers were concretely the following: Managing the looking after the preventive medical care, in general terms, and this was done through my colleague Curic in the entire area. I'm speaking in general terms. And then when it comes to the service for the care of the wounded in the war hospital, because the war hospitals were the most important segment of our healthcare, we had 20 or so such hospitals and they were under the direct commander of my subordinate for the care of the wounded. It was a very important role, a very important link. So this would be one segment of the healthcare. We are talking about huge responsibilities for obtaining medicines, managing people, pursuing healthcare policy, talking to international institutions, talking to the opposite side, attempts to improve and promote the system in general terms, and that was all my responsibility. However, there was also the operational part of the military, and we're talking units here, troops are in the field, which also included healthcare professionals, and I obviously was not in a position to be in command of those people because they had their own commanders in the units, and a doctor should have been, and this is what we fought for, was the assistant of every such commander, and every such commander was directly in command of the doctor. What I'm saying is that I could not, nor did it, I could not command a doctor in the field how to do his job within the unit. This is what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to understand what you were doing as the number one, so let me take the following theoretical cases. Say you visit the Heliodrom camp and you see that there are three doctors there, and there's one doing nothing because he doesn't have enough work. Then you go to Gabela. We all know you didn't go there, but it's a theoretical example. You go to Gabela and you see that there are no doctors. You notice that at the Heliodrom camp there are three doctors, and at Gabela there is none. Was it in your prerogative to say that one of the three doctors of the Heliodrom had to be deployed in Gabela? Was this under your province?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this particular case, the one that you have just mentioned, both centres were under the supervision of the doctors in the military district. In other words, they were covered by the doctors in the military districts, so I could not take somebody from somewhere and transfer them somewhere else. I could issue proposals, I could issue requests. And in this concrete case, if something of that sort had happened, just like I could and was in a position to establish the medical point within the centre, this was our idea. I took all the available men who were not under the direct command of the brigade or military district, and then, in agreement with the doctors in a certain unit, and in this concrete case it was the unit that I spoke about, and if they showed willingness, then we could implement our proposal. It was an extraordinary activity that was not described anywhere. Nobody could envisage that the centres would be opened and that we would have to act accordingly. What we did, we took each case as they came, and we did everything to improve and promote the system that was in place.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to address Dr. Bagaric and say just one sentence in reference to what he said about me implying things. I would like this to be entered into the record and say that General Petkovic's Defence is not implying anything, is not insinuating anything, and if we have a case to prove, we have always tried in this courtroom to explain this very clearly. And if it has been proven that we were not right, we're always prepared to apologise. As far as implications go, I would not go any further into that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have misunderstood you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you may have misunderstood. And I've never believed the course of my -- that my interrogation would take this course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Neither did I.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers kindly slow down and speak one at a time for the benefit of one and all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I showed document 4D1427, from which we could see that in the Republic of Croatia, within the frameworks of the chief of the Main Staff of the Armed Forces and the Health Sector, well, that was there, and I'd like to ask you the following question: In Herceg-Bosna, were there any dilemmas or discussions about organising the Health Sector within the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such discussions and debates. However, if the Main Staff saw the need for -- to have someone directly in the Main Staff, they could have done that. So, therefore, I think that since the Main Staff commanded the military districts and the assistant to the commander of the military district was the doctor, he didn't feel the need in that chain to have somebody in between. Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Bagaric, you told us that all the duties that the health workers had in the military units were professional medical duties, and from that we can conclude that somebody who did not have any medical training could not make the decisions, decisions linked to the field of health. Would that be a correct conclusion on my part?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I go back to the document you showed us a moment ago, and I'll answer your question. There's a document missing here, because I know how the Medical Corps was organised at the time in the Croatian Army. Here, what is lacking is their main medical corps staff which functioned in the same way that we functioned, and I have to say this here and now. That's the truth, and I published this on several occasions in some articles and papers I wrote. So when we established it, we established it taking the example from the Republic of Croatia and some experiences gained there. So in this chart here, we can see that they do have a doctor in the Main Staff, that's true, but they also have another body which is called the Main Medical Staff, led by General Prodan. General Prodan was at the head of that body. And when you ask me, gentlemen, what my tasks and duties were, then, just as it was set out here, I did the equivalent. We copied that system and formation and establishment, with the proviso that we asked the physicians in the Croatian Army -- well, we accepted their proposals for corrections, because they said that certain things needed to be improved and corrected, because to have doctors within logistics was unacceptable, and we found that to be the case, and that is why we endeavoured to pull the doctors out of the Logistics Sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me just say that I'm dealing with the Main Staff in 2008. That's the document, and not at the beginning of the 1990s, and I think that is indubitable, looking at the document, so it was differently organized in Croatia at the beginning of the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise for getting to my feet, but there was a great difference between establishment in wartime and peacetime, so I'd like to thank my learned colleague for clarifying that point just now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Bagaric, let's move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like to propose that too. Let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo is no easy topic, but much better than what we've been discussing so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Look at 4690, please. P4690 is the next document I would like us to look at, which is an agreement on the evacuation of severely sick and wounded persons, which on the Sarajevo -- at Sarajevo Airport was signed by Rasim Delic and Milivoj Petkovic in August, in the presence of Lieutenant-Colonel General Briquemont, Francis Briquemont, Lieutenant-Colonel Francis Briquemont. Now, on page 67 of yesterday's transcript, you mentioned a meeting. Did you discuss this agreement at the meeting or the activities that came under this agreement? If you can't remember, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say this: I was personally called up by General Petkovic to attend a meeting in Sarajevo with Delic, and Briquemont was also there. Now, whether it was this particular meeting, I really can't say, but I do know that those matters were discussed, and others as well. And that's what I said yesterday. So I'm very grateful to General Petkovic, who invited me to go with him, because that gave me a chance to talk to Mr. Delic, and I asked him to allow me, as the head of the Medical Corps, to go to Sarajevo. So that's it. But I can't be quite certain whether that was the occasion or some other occasion, whether Mr. Petkovic might have gone another time and signed another agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the meeting that you mentioned was held at the end of August 1993, whether it did take place?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember, but I'll tell you the location. It was at the airport in Sarajevo, so if that's it, then I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It says: "Done at Sarajevo Airport on the 31st," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you -- I didn't expect your aggressive questions, and they are -- rather, I'm not sure I understood everything. But, yes, I was at that meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, at that meeting General Petkovic was not the number-one man of the HVO, or the second man if we take Mate Boban as being the number-one man; then he was the number-two man. And I have P4493, which is the next document I would like us to look at, and it is information by Slobodan Praljak to UNPROFOR saying that -- let me repeat the number of the document, P4493, 4493. As I was saying, General Praljak is informing UNPROFOR that Milivoj Petkovic has been authorised to negotiate on behalf of the HVO. Now, to the best of your knowledge, Dr. Bagaric, is that what actually happened, that Petkovic did have that authority, regardless of whether he was the commander or deputy commander of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he behaved like somebody who did have the authority, and that allows me to reach my conclusions more than any document would.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you a few questions relating to the detention centres, and I'd like you to look at my third set of documents. And let's look at 2D1537 first, please. You spoke about that document today. And if you look at the lower left-hand corner, it says: "Send to ..." Can you tell us who this report was sent to, can you decipher that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It went to Dr. Curic, as it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the translation of the document in English, what we have written here is it has: "Unclear abbreviations and institution unknown." What does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It refers to our Healthcare Sector, which I headed, and it refers to the Preventive Medical Care Department, led by Dr. Curic, which was -- who acted as additional support to the physicians in the camp and outside the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So this is an abbreviation, this "GSS." The abbreviation is "GSS," is that right, and it stands for "Glavni Saniteski Stozar" [phoen]; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the "GSS" was part of the Health Sector, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next document, 2D1538. I'd like you to tell us who the document was sent to.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same thing, to Mostar, the Main Staff, Mostar. But Mr. Sutalo didn't write the name of the person, but it is to Mr. Curic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I'd like to tell Their Honours, the Prosecutor, and everybody else in the courtroom that this portion of the document has been wrongly interpreted or, rather, translated. In English it says that this report was sent to the Main Staff in Mostar. And I'd also like to draw your attention to the fact that the Stojic Defence, in tabling a request to have this document put on the 65 ter (G) list, wrote that it was a document which was sent to the Main Staff of the HVO in Mostar. And I'm referring to paragraph 5 of the motion that I'm referring to of the 16th of April, and I'm going to quote part of the explanation given by the Stojic Defence in English, and I quote: [In English] "Document 2D01538 is essential to show that reports on the conditions at Gabela were sent directly from the brigades to the Main Staff and were not first routed through the assistant of the head of the Department of the Defence for the Healthcare Sector. The manner by which reports were sent reveals the nature of the links between the healthcare services in brigades and the centralised Healthcare Sector in Mostar." [Interpretation] Now, Dr. Bagaric --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to say -- well, first of all, I'd like to apologise to the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution and my learned friend. There was obviously a mistake in the interpretation, and the assistant -- our assistant was working on the basis of the English version, but we needn't have done it this way. Had the Stojic Defence been apprised of this mistake, we would have put the mistake right and publicly apologised for the mistake. So quite obviously there was a mistake in the translation, which led to further errors being made. I'm sorry that that happened, and had somebody drawn my attention to that, I would have put it right straight away.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric, in view of what Ms. Nozica has just said, I have no more questions regarding this document. I'd just like to say that I thank you for the explanations and that it was, indeed -- and that had it only been a translation mistake, we would have let our colleague know, but as this is contained in the statement of reasons in the motion and signed by Nozica, I did not have time to alert counsel -- lead counsel to this. So it wasn't just a simple mistake, and I apologise if I misunderstood the whole episode.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I say something with respect to this report, Your Honours, because I think it's important. We've discussed the subject at length today, but nonetheless I think what I have to say is important. So might I be allowed to do so? Do I have your permission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, unfortunately you're here to answer questions asked by the counsel. Fine. I'm just telling Ms. Alaburic that she's already used up 52 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Counsel, microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for that information. Yes, I'll get through my cross-examination very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Doctor, talking about the detention centres today, you said something that was particularly important for the Petkovic Defence, so I'm going to ask you to explain what you meant. Did you really say that and mean it or did you misspeak? And it was on page 13 of today's transcript, lines 21 to 25, and page 14, lines 1 to 2. Dr. Bagaric, you said -- well, you roughly said that the instructions about conduct in the detention centres in Croatia, you say, and I quote, that doctors within the units which supervised those centres, and in English this was recorded as "units and military districts to which these centres belonged." You went on to say, Dr. Bagaric, that you don't know whether the Heliodrom was under the authority of the Defence Department or not. Now, did I summarise your statements correctly today about this, on this subject?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to answer the first part of your question or the second?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Both. We have two elements.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what I said, and I stand by that, and I can repeat that now. Yes, I allow for the possibility that I might have added a few words, or I know that everything is weighed up to the extreme here, so I might have made a mistake, but not intentionally, because the nuances are very slight. And my testimony five years ago, for example, if you look at that, when I was here and said what I said, I answered questions from the Prosecutor, and I was completely unprepared for the questions that he asked me, because I was told on the occasion that I was speaking -- that I would be testifying to the general circumstances. And then unprepared -- and what do I mean when I say "unprepared"? It means that a lot of time has gone by, and with the passage of time, I can't remember all the details. But what I did remember, I stated on the occasion, that's what I stated here now, and it is this: As a rule, as a rule, I repeat, for individual prisons, or detention centres, or whatever, or isolation centres, whatever they were called, health protection was provided by doctors from that military district or from individual brigades belonging to that district, together with the physicians who were detainees incarcerated within the centre. Now, later on, with the passage of time, as time went by, along with our support, and when I say "our support," I mean the specialist support provided by Dr. Curic, and I hold that they did their job well, as applied to health protection.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bagaric --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I owe you something.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I owe you my question [as interpreted] about Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. It arises from what you've just said that now you have worded your thesis a bit differently from what you told us before, and now that you're saying that the healthcare was provided to the detainees by the health service of the unit that belonged to the area; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the military unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the military unit that belonged to the area?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is it the right conclusion that you're actually not saying or you don't want to say that that military unit managed or controlled that detention centre?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly, I don't want to say that, because I don't know who controlled and managed that centre, and it really doesn't matter when it comes to the healthcare services provision, which is the only thing that interested me at all in this whole story.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm satisfied with your answer. I was ready to go deeper if your answer was any different. Just one more question that I promised my learned friend Scott. Mr. Bagaric, when you mentioned your visit to -- which is recorded on page 53 of the transcript, you said that to your greatest satisfaction and the satisfaction of the everybody else in the group, it was established that there had been no crimes committed against the civilians in Sovici and that this was confirmed by the Muslims who were isolated in the school in Sovici. Did I understand your words properly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in general terms that would be the correct interpretation of my words, of what I said. However, if the Trial Chamber wants to know more, I can go on and say something more.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is going to be the topic of the Defence case of General Petkovic. When you said that, did you mean that among the civilians, there had been no killed, wounded, or sick, and that there was no need for you or any of your colleagues, health professionals, to take any measures or to take any procedures; is that what you meant when you said that there had been no crimes committed against civilians?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not what I meant, this was not my line of thinking. What was my line of thinking? As I sit here today, I can't say that no civilians were ever wounded there. I really don't know that. However, the Bosniak side, Your Honours, voiced a lot of objections, vis-a-vis Mostar, about the rape of women in Sovici, the killing, the mass murders, and all the hardships and so on and so forth. What they were saying was this, You want to go to Kostajnica, where we did what we did, and they knew what we had done. At the same time, they asked from us to allow them to go to Sovici, and they accused us of doing things there. I really didn't know at the time whether things had been done or not, and when we arrived in Sovici, and when we went there together, Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Halilovic, we got to the school and then we saw people there who were incarcerated in that school, but there was no -- the extent of the crime that was implicated, which was confirmed by the civilians and which we were able to establish, and it made me happy to establish that. And on that occasion, I noticed a great deal of dissatisfaction on the part of the Bosniak Muslims who were incarcerated in the school, but that was addressed at Halilovic, because the way they were talking to him was, You promised us help, help never arrived, and I believe that they meant in military terms because some soldiers had been killed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bagaric, I would like to thank you. We will continue during General Petkovic's case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll see about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing resumes, and I think it is D3 now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Dr. Bagaric.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: First of all, let's wage a little war. I'm going to take you back to 1992, to October 1992. Let's talk about Jajce and the evacuation of the wounded and the sick and civilians from Jajce at the moment when Jajce was about to fall. You've already spoken about that in answering my learned friend Nozica's questions. This was on page 38 and also on page 50. First of all, let me ask you this: In the chief examination, you said that the evacuation of civilians, the wounded, the women and the children, was done by armoured buses?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one or two, not many.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I did not mean -- I did not have in mind any quantity. So you're saying one or two buses?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Where did the armoured buses come from?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a time when things were very hard and the wounded had to be evacuated. I suppose that the Trial Chamber doesn't know what Jajce looks like. It's a gorge some ten kilometres long, and it was impossible to evacuate.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Please, could you slow down, because things have to be recorded.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was impossible to evacuate the wounded by any other means. We could not use helicopters because we did not have any. It had to be done by road, and the road that we had to take, we -- me and my colleague doctors, it was some 20 kilometres long through that gorge, and there was a threat of people being killed or wounded, and that's why we turned for assistance to General Prodan in the Republic of Croatia. I knew him personally. And then I believe that he and some other people -- I don't remember any details. I believe that Mr. Praljak also participated in requesting that assistance. We were provided with the vehicle, and we used the vehicle to evacuate the wounded, the civilians, and the soldiers, both Bosniak, Muslims, and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. This is what I wanted to hear. We are going to go through the documents which are in the sequence that I will be using them. Before we tackle documents, I would like to ask you something else. You also mentioned Dr. Kolak on examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you this: Do you know that in the operation that took place in Jajce, and within the framework of the Medical Service, Dr. Gveric was very active?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: There was also Jadranko [as interpreted] Barisic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Dr. Josip Barisic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a doctor in Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. And now could you please look at document 3D01238. It says here Dr. Josip Barisic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: This is the doctor that you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: This is his report in which he requests urgent evacuation of the wounded?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And now I would ask you to turn to the next document.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Help me, for God's sake.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers not overlap, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You're saying that there is a cry for help because the situation was difficult?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a cry for help because they were seized with uncertainty, the doctors and everybody. The times were really very unfortunate.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: When I'm waiting, I'm waiting for the answer to be recorded. I don't want us to overlap. Yes, I agree that that was indeed the case, and this transpires only too well from the document. And now could you please look at the following document, 3D02819. The document is addressed to Major Ivo Prodan. Dr. Bagaric, is that you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Dr. Markunovic in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Dr. Dzambas in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And Dr. Saric in Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Again, this did Dr. Josip Barisic's report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What is it that Dr. Barisic is saying in this report? Again, this is a cry for help, is it not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's solely post festum, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So this is a statement that the doomsday or the judgement day has taken place. Can you please now look at 3D03527. Look at the second page of the document.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did you draft the document? You did, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If this is an integral document, and I believe it is, then, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You did. And you submit a report to the head of Defence, Mr. Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: About what?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the evacuation of the wounded from Jajce which was taking place, and this is what it refers to. I can't remember the details at the moment, but I know, in general terms, what the report is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And you were the one who drafted it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was either me, by myself, or together with somebody. I signed it, and I am responsible for it, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: An integral part of the document is the following report on the following page. Is the handwriting at the bottom yours?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, it is my handwriting. I laughed because I don't understand where you got this paper from.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It's an integral part of the document, is it not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. We have now completed the story of Jajce, which was when Jajce fell on the 22nd of -- 29th of October, 1992. You have spoken about the Medical Service, and I would now kindly ask you to look at document 3D03528.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The title is "Medical Report"?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Who was it who issued such reports?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was drafted in the Operations Zone of South-Eastern Herzegovina, the medical service of the operations zone, and I believe that this was done by the doctor. Let's not go over the same ground again. Let's just say that he was in charge of medical services in the operations zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. And again he sent that report to you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Also to the head of the Medical Service, Dr. Burkic [phoen], and the commander of the operations zone in South-East Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the military commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And this is a report about Operation Bura?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can we see from this document when the preparations for operation Bura actually started?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 22nd of October, 1992. I believe that's that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So the report was sent. The operation was already underway, and these are the [indiscernible] of the operation that was underway?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What was typical of this operation was the fact that unfortunately, according to what I know and remember, ended in a very unfortunate manner, when it came to the HVO, because the commander, Mr. Simovic, got killed, and this is what I remember the most. I believe that we suffered a lot of losses, and I believe that you can see that in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, you can see that in this document. Can we then conclude that -- or, rather, first of all, can you tell us where the Operation Bura or Tempest was taking place, for the Trial Chamber and the other sides in the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was personally not engaged in this operation, but I know that this operation took place during the war against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: This means that Croats and Muslims, Bosniaks, were together?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can we then agree that this was in the south, that it was around Storac [phoen], Dobroskavis [phoen] Plateau and Podvelezje?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You see that the commander of Medical Department, Edin Obradovic, which confirms exactly what you have just said.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's the one who signed that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And he's a Bosniak, is he not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is. I suppose so, judging by the name.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap once again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Edin Obradovic could be a child from a mixed marriage, but in any case his name is Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: If we follow the list, we can see that the dead and wounded were both Muslims and Croats and that they had fought together; wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you mention Mr. Bozan Simovic, which is on the last page of this document, it says here the names of the killed, Bozan Simovic, this is a report of the 1st Herzegovina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Go to the last page of the Croatian text.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but because he was the symbol of an honest and courageous soldier, one unit bears his name, and I believe that the barracks also bear his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, the barracks also bear his name. We're going to skip the following document because my learned friend Senka has already dealt with it. It is about the ambulance that was given to Sally Backer. We'll now move to document 3D03525, which is a story which was published in the professional magazine "Lancet." Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What can you tell us about this article? It was authored by Richard Horton. Do you know who he is? And there is a reference to you in this article.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very, very valuable article. At least it's important to me. It was published in one of the most influential and the most quoted, as the Trial Chamber certainly knows, medical magazines. "Lancet" is a very well-known magazine, next to the British Medical Journal, is one of the most influential medical magazines. The editor-in-chief of "Lancet," Mr. Richard Horton, toured the area after the war, and he spoke to some of the doctors that had been engaged during the war in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well, and that's why he published two articles. You have just one here. The title is "Imprints of War in Bosnia and Croatia." There are two articles, and one refers to Croatia and the other to Bosnia-Herzegovina. In this article, he actually speaks about doctors and how they have to be far-sighted and look in the future. This is what I tried to tell you yesterday, and I probably bore you out with that, but this is what I always firmly believed. I still believe it. He quotes Nietzsche and he finishes the article on that note. He says that the doctors are the ones who have, during the war -- think differently, behave differently, and then analyse the behaviour and the experience. And based on their experience, they have to improve humanitarian knowledge for the future, help with the prevention of war as a phenomenon, as an evil phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: A reference is made here to the document that you drafted together with Ms. Nozica, which is your letter to UNPROFOR asking for points to be set up. This is mentioned in the introduction of the article, your attempts and your desire to do something. You didn't draft it with Ms. Nozica, but you talked about it with her?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what the doctors heard. They heard about our activities, the activities that we participated in, and that's why he wanted to talk to me, and I showed him a copy of that document. I had it on me because I was working on my Master's thesis, themed [as interpreted] around the organisation of the medical care of the HVO. He deemed the document very important, and I'm very, very grateful to him for having quoted that document in his article. And as a matter of fact, he bases the article on that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to one more sentence. I know that you are not going to find it easy to talk about it, but still I believe it's important to talk about this. Mr. Horton says that on the 12th of April, 1992, your brother was killed, and although he was killed as a result of Serb shelling in Surica [phoen], that you never blamed the Serbs; you blamed the war for everything that happened.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, this is an event that made a very big impression on me, when something like that happened, when you yourself become a victim, then everybody's hardship becomes your own hardship, and you are able to empathise with people better and you are able to forgive more. Of course, it has made a huge, big impression on the rest of my life.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And now let's go to document 3D03526.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm especially proud of this article, especially proud of this article which was published in the "Military Medicine," the leading magazine which deals with war or military medicine, and that's very important. However, even more important for me is the fact that the signatories of the article are myself and Professor Reuben Eldar, or the other way around, Professor Eldar and myself, and Professor Eldar is the best expert on military medicine. He is a specialist in public healthcare and my mentor, so it is my great honour that I had an opportunity to meet this person and to author such an important publication in such an important magazine.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You know that our time is very valuable. I still need to ask you something about the article. I can't quote all of it. However, in one part of the article, a reference is made to the routes of evacuation of the wounded and sick by air, by road, and by the sea, and in one part it is said that the only possibility of air-lift and air evacuation was to Central Bosnia because that was the only part of Bosnia where a helicopter could land and take off from?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
