utterances.text: One of the way -- elements of the efficiency of the service is the speed of the time in which you can reach wounded or sick, and the second element is whether they can be treated. My dear colleagues in the field, within the first hour, did manage to reach the sick and the wounded and provide them with first aid, even bring them to hospitals. However, it was also important, after that, what to do after that. For example, the hospital in Bila was a hospital which was not equipped for final treatment, and that's why the helicopter flights were very important, and that is why the gentlemen who were present here, there is almost not a single one who did not participate with their support, with their approval for such flights that served to transport the wounded. And the story about the dear lady Sally Backer is of the same kind. She wanted to help the Muslims on the east bank, but she realised that the Croats in Central Bosnia had a similar if not a bigger problem, because nobody paid -- no media paid so much attention to them, and that is something sometimes very important, and that's why she carried out the helicopter evacuation. She had been instrumental during the period of time when we could not carry out evacuation. She was the one who was instrumental in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you remember the names of any of the pilots who drove the helicopters or is that too much to ask 16 years on?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I do remember one in particular, because he had an interesting name. His name was Mr. Yugoslav. And I also remember the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Natalija?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, him, too, but I had somebody else in mind. I know the man, but I just can't tell you the name just now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you something else about this article and then one more document, and that will be it. In that same article, which doesn't seem to be -- the pages of which don't seem to be numbered, but before the section dealing with the different aspects of the operation or mode of operation, you said, and you said that during the examination-in-chief today, that the Medical Corps was formed before the brigades?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You say that in this article, too, don't you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that was a phenomenon of sorts. We did it in comparison to what the Israelis did in their wars and how some other people organised this. We made this comparison, comparative analysis, and in a way it is a phenomenon of sorts, but it was in fact the result of an impossible situation that we found ourselves in in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Croats there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. And apart from that, you say that the Medical Corps did not become the official part of the military staff, that they were two bodies, two separate bodies, which necessarily cooperated closely, but that within the HVO they were at the same level, they had the same level, the same hierarchal level, and that was the phenomenon in military medicine?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about -- yes, that's true, that's quite true, and we're talking about the time when I, in formal terms, was appointed chief of the Main Medical Corps, and at the same time the Main Staff of the HVO didn't exist yet. It might appear strange, but that's how it was. And then by appointment of the Chief of Staff, we maintained this high level independently with the Medical Corps being put -- established, and with the Ministry coming in, everybody took their own part. So that is my answer that I tried to give earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you another question. It is this, a practical question, so that we can understand what's going on here: A doctor, in war --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel repeat her question?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What I was saying: A doctor in Rama drinks every day, is not near the brigade. He doesn't pay attention to whether they have enough medicines, sanitary material, and so on. He refuses -- he's unkempt, he's not properly washed and combed, and he refuses to examine a patient. What happens?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know of any such person, but if he was in a war hospital, then the commander of the war hospital will call him up, and it was linked to our service, the service that saw to the care of the wounded. But if he was in a brigade, then the brigade commander would call him to task, and he can --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can he replace him?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: When the brigade medical corps was established?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But until that happened, we had the heads of civilian medical centres who took over the role, who took that role over from us or, rather, from the Main Medical Corps. They were head of the municipal staffs. So that was the very beginning of the beginning, and it was a primitive type of organisation in the sense of establishing both the army and the medical corps within it, and that's why it was quite special, because we had special circumstances. And during the war, we were left without any communication with the large medical centres, so we had to rely exclusively on what we doctors call primary healthcare, that level; that is to say, the doctors who were in the health centres. There were no surgeons in those health centres, there were no anesthesiologists, because that's not where they worked, and the few surgeons and anesthesiologists we had, we had one anesthesiologist, they worked in two hospitals, in Mostar and in Livno, and many people had already left. So we were facing a very, very difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, we are aware of that. Now, I'm going to ask the usher's assistance, and we'd like to look at 2D00412, the next document, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean in this binder?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: No, not in my binder, but it was a document that came up during the examination-in-chief. It is your order dated -- I'll give you the date in just a moment. The date is September, the 28th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And the same document is 2D00131, but that's the 26th of November, 1993, but we're going to deal with the first one. First things first. So would you turn to page 2, please. In English, it is also on page 2, and the English document is three pages long. And I'm going to ask you, first of all: Who was this document sent to? Or, rather, would you agree with me that the document was not sent to the Main Staff of the HVO, this particular order?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, it wasn't sent to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you explain why?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we are addressing the units here, the units on the ground, and all those who can influence changes in the field of healthcare or whatever, and those elements that could have an influence on health, but weren't under doctors' orders, for example, food, equipment, clothing and so on for the people, we are addressing the commanders of the operative zones. The commanders of the operative zones, that's who we're addressing here as military organs, military formations, who can have direct links to the brigades, because there were doctors there who were involved from inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: But the Main Staff knew nothing about this; right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this and -- they needn't have known about this order of ours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right. Now let's take a look at point 14. It says for -- as far as the organisation of the work of the medical check-points is concerned: "The heads of the Medical Corps of the HVO brigades are directly responsible to me, as are the wardens of the mentioned centres." So you compiled this order, and who was responsible if this order was not put into practice? Who was held responsible, and to whom were they responsible?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here I state that -- well, I didn't have time to elaborate this document, but, anyway, after gaining an insight into the situation and having talked to the doctors who were there, we saw that there were problems, and we sized up the situation and wanted to improve it, to do what we could to improve it. So we set up medical corps posts or -- posts, yes, and people who were in charge of the medical side of matters, and here I say the heads of the centres, the wardens of the centres. That was a little too ambitious, I feel, but that's what it says on this document. And, anyway, there were a lot of areas that were not strictly medical, but that did have an effect on health, such as food, clothing, for people in the centre, and that couldn't -- problems of that kind couldn't be resolved by the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It regarded a broader area?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, logistics in general terms, any logistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right. I have no further questions, and that completes my cross-examination. Thank you. Thank you, Dr. Bagaric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to apologise. I would like to say that on page 96, line 13, the witness said it's logistics of the operative zone, the brigade on any logistics, so the witness can confirm that that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, logistics, as such, per se.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, earlier on the counsel for General Praljak talked about 3D3526, which you drafted on the medical unit during the war, 1993 to 1995. I carefully read that document which you co-drafted, and you wrote, and that struck me, that according to the statistics, 11 per cent of the wounded were taken to the military hospitals, while for the sake of comparison, in the Sinai, I'm sure that you are referring to the war between Israel and Egypt, over 50 per cent were taken to military hospitals, and you talk about the mortality rate among the wounded. And you said that in the Croatian military hospitals, they ranged between 80 and 8 per cent, and you compare that rate to other figures you had; for example, that of the Beirut American Hospital and Israeli hospitals, and from that you draw the conclusion that this was functioning well. I read this, and it occurred to me that we heard witnesses on the East Mostar Military Hospital. And you know as well as I do that this East Mostar Military Hospital had been established by the BiH in order to treat the wounded from the Mostar front as well as the civilians. We've also seen videos here. We could show you a video, but let's not do that. And I had the feeling, viewing that video and reading the document, that the mortality rate in East Mostar was definitely higher than the 8 per cent of the Croatian military hospitals. So in your paper, why did you not go into the question of the East Mostar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, the reason is this: We were dealing with the Croatian medical bodies or health service in Bosnia and Herzegovina and organisation within it, so I couldn't take the question of the Mostar Hospital on the east bank because it didn't belong to the HVO. This article refers to the Medical Corps of the HVO, that's what it's about, and that's what I dealt with, and that's what it says in its title. But you noticed full well that when, all things considered, we were very successful in caring and treating our wounded, but that was how it functioned overall at a general level. But, of course, in each individual hospital, that wasn't always the case. For example, in Bila, that wasn't what it was like. It was an average, a generalisation, and this information was taken from papers published in scholarly journals on individual hospitals and in individual hospitals. Each of these institutions had their own journals and published their own data. And you know this approach. It was a summary, a precis, but we weren't able to deal with the Mostar hospital on the east bank because it didn't belong to the Health Service of the HVO, and it wouldn't have been believable, valid. Why didn't we deal with the Sarajevo hospitals? Then we would have -- the paper would have been entitled "The Health Service in Bosnia-Herzegovina." Here we only dealt with the Croatian part of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Final question: You've talked about Bila. I've read in a document, and I can't remember its number, that this Bila Hospital served 200.000 inhabitants. This is what the document states. In terms of, Doctor to population ratio, did you have the feeling that the hospitals under Croatian control in Bosnia-Herzegovina were not as well off as other hospitals in other countries, or even hospitals in the BiH area? Was it a good ratio, a not-so-good ratio? So can you comment on the ratio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, absolutely inferior. Now, why? Here's why: Because -- well, not in all cases, the BH Army had some hospitals, too, which were in some far-off place without any possibility of communication, and hospitals like that then were similar to the situation in Bila, but it's very important to mention here that the large medical centres which existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, such as Tuzla - Tuzla's a big town with several thousand health workers - then you have Zenica, another big centre, Sarajevo, they all remained on territory that was under the control of the BH Army, and they already had their hospitals, hospitals that had been opened before the war both to Serbs and Croats and everyone, and now suddenly they became inaccessible to the Croats. We wouldn't have built a hospital in Bila had we been able to go just a few kilometres away and use the Travnik Hospital, for example, because Bila, in fact, was a municipality which belonged to Travnik. They had a large hospital, a modern hospital there, which had been in existence for many years, with an expert staff, well trained, and compared to them our position was quite inferior. And if I might be allowed to make my own observations, that's my own opinion, I am convinced that those cries for help of ours, when we asked that we work together in Mostar, that they were read by the army as meaning if we accept that, there was no logic for blocking the inflow of patients and staff and Croats who had until then been treated in the hospitals under their control, and this would have contributed quite a great deal to putting an end to the conflict and also to taking care of all our people up there. So I do believe that they just let things stand to see if they could take control of Central Bosnia, as that was a more important goal than to deal with the question of the wounded Muslims and Bosniaks on the east bank of Mostar. That is what I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One final, final question. We've heard witnesses about this, and the counsels also talked about the departure of the JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina, taking away all the arms and ammunition, artillery, et cetera, and this question was never asked to anyone: As far as you know, the military hospitals under JNA control, when the JNA left, did they take away all the military equipment, all the resuscitation material? Did they -- all the equipment, did they take all that with them or did they leave everything intact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, when it comes to Bosnia-Herzegovina, then, as far as I know, that was only the case of one particular hospital, and that was the hospital in Sarajevo, the former military hospital there which I know very well, because I studied in Sarajevo. It was a modern institution. And I think that later on, after the war, when I worked in Sarajevo in the Health Ministry with the head of the hospital, in talking to him, I heard that the hospital had been emptied out. That's the expression he used. But I know full well that in Croatia, in Zagreb, for example, and some negotiations and agreements under pressure from the international community, they failed to do that in the Zagreb military Hospital. But as to the other military hospitals in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I don't think there were any, there were none. What did exist were the large centres such as Banja Luka, Prijedor, and so on, which remained under the control of the Serbian Army and, as such, were not accessible to Croats, except during the war, once again, under very strange circumstances when the Croats were in an open conflict, and the Muslim Bosniaks as well, and the Croats had no choice. And then they had to pay very dearly for their medical treatment, which was provided to them in certain localities by the Serb side. For example, this was the situation in Kiseljak, Zepce, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I almost forgot to ask D5 whether you had questions for Mr. Curic [as interpreted]. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have no questions for this witness. We would like to thank him for coming to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, we have another three minutes. We're not going to give you the floor now. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to correct something on page 101, line 7. The name of the witness was wrong there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'd like to ask the Prosecution again, are you going to start tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I can start now, Mr. President, if you'd like, but I do see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's another three minutes left, so it's better to start tomorrow. Fine, so we'll start tomorrow. As you know, the hearing will take place in the afternoon, so, Witness, please be back at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon. I would like to thank everyone, and let's meet tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
